title: Word Roots, Prefixes, and Suffixes

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the root as the foundation of a house: everything else is built on top of it and depends on it. In 'cardiology,' the root 'cardi' means heart, so whatever prefix or suffix you add around it, the word is still fundamentally about the heart.

### Question 2

A prefix is like a label stuck on the front of a box before you look inside. 'Sub-' up front tells you 'under,' so 'subcutaneous' means under the skin. The label sits at the front and shapes how you read what comes next.

### Question 3

The suffix is like the ending of a story that tells you what happened. In 'arthritis,' 'arthr' is the joint and '-itis' at the end tells you it is inflamed. The ending finishes the thought about the body part.

### Question 4

The combining vowel is like a drop of oil that lets two gears turn together smoothly. 'Gastr' plus 'scopy' is a mouthful, so we slide an 'o' in: 'gastroscopy.' The 'o' does not mean anything; it just makes the word roll off your tongue.

### Question 5

If you kept the 'o' you would get 'cardi-o-itis,' with vowels bumping together, which sounds clumsy. So when the ending already starts with a vowel, the 'o' steps aside and we write 'carditis.' But when the ending starts with a consonant, the 'o' stays to keep things smooth, as in 'cardiology.'

### Question 6

'-itis' is the alarm that says a part is red, hot, and swollen, like an inflamed sore throat. '-ectomy' is the action word meaning a surgeon removed the part. One tells you there is a problem; the other tells you the part was taken out.

### Question 7

Picture 'hyper' like a hyperactive puppy bouncing up high above everything, and 'hypo' like something sunk down low in a hole. 'Hyper' is too much or too high; 'hypo' is too little or too low. They are exact opposites even though they look almost the same.

### Question 8

Snap the word apart like building blocks: 'gastr' is the stomach block, 'enter' is the intestine block, and '-itis' is the 'it's inflamed' block, with a little 'o' holding them together. Put them back and you get 'the stomach and intestines are inflamed.'

### Question 9

'-megaly' comes from the Greek for 'large,' like the 'mega' in mega-size. So when you see it on the end of an organ word, picture that organ swollen larger than normal. 'Cardiomegaly' is a heart that has grown too big.

### Question 10

The root 'dermat' stays as skin no matter what. To change what is happening to the skin, you swap the ending. Trade '-logy' (studying it) for '-itis' (it's inflamed), and the word now says the skin is inflamed instead of being studied.

### Question 11

The little 'a-' or 'an-' at the front works like a 'no' sign. Add it and it means 'not there' or 'missing.' Take it off 'anemia' and you lose the whole point, which is that something in the blood is lacking. Small prefix, big job.

### Question 12

Take each word apart like a puzzle. 'Pericarditis' is 'around' + heart + 'inflamed,' so it is the sac around the heart being inflamed. 'Electrocardiogram' joins two roots, electricity and heart, with '-gram' meaning a written record, so it is a tracing of the heart's electrical activity. Different builds, same rules.
